name: Melodrama
blurb: Moustaches, mortgages and a 4:15 that is never late for a tragedy.

setup.logline: The mortgage falls due at noon, and the parlour clock has, suspiciously, started to hurry.

lines.text: The mortgage falls due at noon, {lead}. Pay it, or the parlour, the piano and the cat's little cushion are mine.
But it is barely nine o'clock, {villain}!
Look at the {object}. Look at it very, very carefully.
It says noon. It has said noon since breakfast. I think it is frightened of you.

setup.logline: A letter arrives from the sailor Jack, three years late and still slightly damp.

lines.text: A letter from Jack! Posted three years ago, and only now has it stopped being damp.
I fetched it from the river. The river had already read it. It was very moved.
'Dearest, I return on the 4:15, with a ring, a medal and a very small parrot.'
The 4:15. How interesting. I shall be on the platform, wearing my best moustache.

setup.logline: Papa's funeral tea is served, and the sausage rolls are vanishing at a speed Papa would have admired.

lines.text: Papa is cold in the ground, and the tea is warm on the table. Such is life, and such are sausage rolls.
My deepest condolences, {lead}. My deeper condolences about the rent. May I have a sausage roll?
I have eaten four sausage rolls in Papa's memory. He would have wanted me to be strong.
He would have wanted you to stop at three.

setup.logline: Papa's study has been locked since the funeral, and the landlord has begun wearing the key on a chain.

lines.text: Papa's study has been locked since the funeral. What is behind that {object}, {villain}?
Nothing. Paperwork. Dust. A small and entirely legal fire.
I can smell it from here. Paper, and wax, and the word 'whereas'.
Heel, {fool}. Sit. Go and be loyal somewhere else.

setup.logline: The landlord proposes marriage, citing an enormous fortune and, in a smaller voice, a patched elbow.

lines.text: Marry me, {lead}, and I shall make you the owner of an enormous fortune. Ignore the patched elbow; it is fashionable.
I would sooner marry the hat stand!
The hat stand is flattered, but it has asked me to say it is spoken for.
Then I shall wait. I am patient, {lead}. My moustache is not.

complication.logline: The heiress is tied to the railway line, and the 4:15 has never once been late for a tragedy.

lines.text: Unhand me, {villain}! This rope is made of knots and bad intentions!
The 4:15 is four minutes away, {lead}. It has never once been late for a tragedy.
I will save you! Right after I find a knife. Or a pair of scissors. Or, failing those, teeth.
Teeth are fine, {fool}. Please chew faster.

complication.logline: A blizzard of torn paper sweeps the moor, and the Faithful Hound starts to sing.

lines.text: The moor is wide, the night is cold, and my slippers are made entirely of hope.
I shall sing to keep your spirits up. 'Oh, the wind, the wind, the wind, and then the wind again.'
Stop that. I am trying to menace you through a blizzard, and you are making it cosy.
It is rather cosy, actually. Do go on, {fool}.

complication.logline: The landlord offers the Faithful Hound a pork pie in exchange for one small betrayal.

lines.text: {fool}, I have a pork pie. A whole one. It is yours if you tell me where the will is hidden.
I could never betray {lead}. I am loyal. I am extremely loyal. How big is the pie?
{fool}! You are my last friend on this wretched moor!
I know. I know. It is a very good pie.

complication.logline: A duel is fought on the cliff edge with one rubber sword, one teapot and no clear rules.

lines.text: En garde, {lead}! I have not duelled since the incident with the pudding.
I have never held a sword! I have held a teapot, once, in anger.
Use the teapot! No, the sword! No, the teapot! Please choose, I am extremely frightened.
Do hold still, {lead}. I am trying to be terrifying, and you are being difficult with a teapot.

complication.logline: A kindly widow offers the heiress shelter, a bonnet and an unexpectedly robust moustache.

lines.text: Good evening, dear. I am an entirely different person: a kindly widow who knits and owns no railways.
What a relief! You have such a lovely bonnet. And such a... remarkable upper lip.
Hereditary. Come, let me take you somewhere with a great deal of rope.
The widow is so kind! Why is the rope always the first thing on the menu?

reversal.logline: The will is found in the least-opened book in the library, and it leaves everything to the cat.

lines.text: I have found the will! It was inside 'Sensible Investments, Volume Nine.' Nobody ever opens that one.
Read it aloud, {fool}!
'To my beloved daughter I leave my blessing and my watch. The fortune goes in trust to...' the cat.
The cat? Then I demand to be appointed the cat's guardian. Nobody tell the cat.

reversal.logline: The landlord's terrible secret is revealed: a very large hat, and nowhere else to live.

lines.text: I never wanted your parlour, {lead}. I wanted a parlour. Any parlour. I have been living in a very large hat.
A hat, {villain}?
It is draughty. The brim leaks. I keep the {object} in it, for company.
I will fetch you a blanket, {villain}. Then I shall go back to hating you. It is a busy week.

reversal.logline: The Wronged Heiress learns that the true heiress is, in fact, the Faithful Hound.

lines.text: The birthmark, {lead}! The one shaped like a small crown! You do not have it. {fool} does.
That is a rash. I have had it since the bath.
All these years I walked you, I fed you, I gave you the good biscuits...
Then I shall be generous in victory. You may keep the other biscuits.

reversal.logline: The landlord throws the will on the fire, only to learn that the Faithful Hound has already eaten it.

lines.text: Behold, {lead}! I cast the will upon the fire! Now your claim is ash!
Wait. I have already eaten it. I got there first. It tasted of wax and legal destiny.
Then the will lives on, inside {fool}!
Then we shall all have to wait for nature to take its course. Everyone sit down. Nobody speak.

reversal.logline: The library lamp goes out, and the heiress embraces the wrong moustache.

lines.text: The lamp has gone out! Jack, my darling, is that you in the dark?
...Possibly.
I knew it! Kiss me, before the 4:15 does something dramatic!
Unhand {lead}! That is not Jack! Jack has a parrot! This one only has a faint smell of wax!

twist.logline: The grave begins to move. It has Papa's shoes.

lines.text: {lead}, the grave is moving. I am not saying it is Papa. I am saying it has his shoes.
Papa! You are alive!
Impossible. I paid for that headstone. I paid extra for the cherub.
Papa says he was hiding from the bank. He says the soil was surprisingly good for his back.

twist.logline: Inside the locket is a baby portrait. The baby has a moustache, and it is the landlord's.

lines.text: In my mother's locket there is a portrait of a baby. A baby with... a moustache.
That is my baby picture, {lead}. It was taken the day we were separated at the fair.
You are siblings! That explains the rent, the railway line, and the matching ears.
I was lonely. It is how I show affection. I am told it is not widely recommended.

twist.logline: A ghost rises over Papa's grave. It has a tail, and a bedsheet on backwards.

lines.text: Woooo. I am the ghost of Papa. I am extremely dead and not at all a hound under a sheet.
That ghost has a tail. I can see the tail.
The dead wag too, {villain}. It is well documented.
Thank you, {fool}. Your sheet is on backwards, but I am deeply moved.

twist.logline: The bottle that killed Papa is found, and it is signed, with a flourish, by the landlord.

lines.text: I have found the bottle that killed Papa. It says 'Poison' on the front and 'Landlord's Own' on the back.
Anyone could have written that. Anyone with my handwriting.
It is signed, {villain}. 'Yours sincerely, the villain.'
I sign everything. It is a compulsion. It is in the moustache.

twist.logline: The moustache comes off, and the landlord turns out to be the sailor Jack.

lines.text: Wait. If I take off the moustache, {villain} is Jack. {villain} is the sailor. I am so confused.
Jack?! You posted the letter, you wrote the mortgage, and you tied me to the tracks?
I was lonely at sea, {lead}. I got into property. The parrot was a separate decision.
I am going to need everybody to sit down, and also the parrot.

finale.logline: The landlord is defeated and begins to die, in no particular hurry.

lines.text: Aargh! You have bested me, {lead}! I am slain! I am dying! I am dying slightly more!
Is that the end of it, {villain}?
No. There is a speech. Gather round. It is mostly apologies and a recipe.
Please die, {villain}. The 4:15 is in the next scene and it hates to be kept waiting.

finale.logline: The landlord's fiendish chandelier trap goes off, and the chandelier picks the landlord.

lines.text: Stand upon the grand staircase, {lead}, beneath the chandelier! My fiendish contraption will finally...
Cutting the rope, {lead}! Brace yourselves!
{fool}, no! {villain} is the one standing under...
I am wearing the chandelier. I came down the stairs in it. I would like it noted that I have never been so well lit.

finale.logline: The parlour is saved, the mortgage is torn, and the wedding has a bride, a vicar and no agreed groom.

lines.text: The parlour is saved, the mortgage is torn, and Papa is merely resting. Let the wedding begin!
Who is the groom? I put myself forward. I have a moustache and a good deal of remorse.
The hat stand has also put itself forward. We have agreed to let the audience decide.
Then let us sing, and settle it during the second verse.

finale.logline: The 4:15 arrives early for once, through the castle gates, driven by a very small parrot.

lines.text: Hark! The 4:15! It is early, for the first time in its life, and it is coming through the front door!
Jack? Is that you at last, on the footplate?
It is a parrot, {lead}. The train is being driven by a very small parrot.
The parrot is doing wonderfully. It has only run over the one flowerbed.

finale.logline: With the plot exhausted, the cast appeals directly to the audience, and a hat goes round.

lines.text: Friends, neighbours, patrons of {town}: the mortgage remains unpaid, and the 4:15 has been cancelled.
It is true. I have no more moustache to twirl. I do, however, have a hat. Pass it round.
Every penny goes to the parlour. One penny to me, for the ham.
And should we not be saved by the end of the hat, we shall simply perform it all again.

name: Farce
blurb: Doors. So many doors, and everyone arriving at once.

setup.logline: A visitor arrives to read the gas meter and is instantly mistaken for the vicar.

lines.text: Good morning. I am only here to read the gas meter.
The vicar! At last! The wedding is in twelve minutes and we have not yet found a bride.
Wedding? What wedding? I only came to return an umbrella!
I am not a vicar. But I will certainly consider it, if the hat is good.

setup.logline: The Flustered Hero has invited both fiancées to lunch, and describes this as a system.

lines.text: I have invited my fiancée to lunch. And my other fiancée. They arrive at one. I am perfectly calm.
Splendid. And which of them knows about the other?
Neither. That is the foundation of the whole arrangement.
I am not engaged to anyone. May I sit by the window? I should like to be completely uninvolved.

setup.logline: Lunch for twelve, four chairs, and a soufflé that must on no account be sat on.

lines.text: Lunch for twelve and four chairs. We shall sit in shifts. I have drawn up a rota.
And the soufflé? It must not be disturbed, or it will fall, and so shall I.
I am sitting on the soufflé. It was the only free chair. It is very warm and surprisingly supportive.
Nobody move. It may yet rise.

setup.logline: A telegram arrives reading 'Believe nothing. Burn this.' and is burned before anyone finishes the sentence.

lines.text: A telegram! 'ARRIVING TODAY STOP BELIEVE NOTHING STOP BURN THIS STOP.' Who sent it?
Not me. Probably. It is in my handwriting, but I was very tired that week.
I have burned it, as instructed. It was easier than reading it.
Excellent. Now nobody knows what we are hiding. Least of all us.

setup.logline: The brother-in-law begins a welcome speech, and the doorbell keeps rewriting it.

lines.text: Friends, welcome to a weekend of peace, quiet and uncomplicated relationships. Is that the doorbell?
No. Nobody is expected. We shall not answer. It is a draught with ambitions.
That is the fourth draught. I am letting them in, and then hiding in the umbrella stand.
I said uncomplicated. I should like that on the record.

complication.logline: Seven doors, one corridor, and everyone certain that the exit is behind somebody else's.

lines.text: Quick, through here! No, not here, that is the cupboard. Which one is the corridor?
You are in the corridor. You have been in it for two minutes. It is simply very long.
I have gone through the same door four times. I keep coming out of the other one. It is thrilling.
The corridor is round, {fool}. Somebody built this house in a circle, to be spiteful.

complication.logline: The hero poses as the maid to avoid a fiancée, and the brother-in-law develops a weakness.

lines.text: I am Marguerite, the maid. I am not {lead}. {lead} left in a cab, with a cold. I have checked the mirror.
Marguerite! What a coincidence. I have a weakness for maids and a second, smaller weakness for lies.
Marguerite, the mirror is on your side, but you do have a moustache. I say it kindly. Put it away before lunch.
It is a family trait. We are a very hairy and extremely modest family.

complication.logline: The only chair in the corridor has wheels, and sitting down is everyone's only alibi.

lines.text: Sit, {lead}! Nobody can accuse a person who is sitting. It is the first law of hospitality.
The {object} is moving! The {object} is leaving the corridor, with me on it!
I will catch you! There! Oh. I have caught the {object}. You are now over there, sitting in a plant.
Well, at least the plant is not accusing anybody.

complication.logline: A tureen of soup begins its journey up the stairs and has not yet been seen to arrive.

lines.text: Soup for the bedroom! I have carried the tureen up all eighteen stairs without spilling a drop.
Admirable. You are, however, holding only the lid.
I am holding... only the lid. Where is the soup?
Down the banister, I should think. Listen. It is still going.

complication.logline: Three secret notes arrange three private meetings in the same bedroom at the same time.

lines.text: A note under the door: 'Meet me in the blue bedroom at three. Come alone. Bring nothing.' I am touched.
I also received a note. 'The blue bedroom at three. Come alone. Bring snacks.'
Mine says 'The blue bedroom at three. Come alone. Tell no one.' I have told nobody. I have only told you.
So three people will be alone together in the blue bedroom at three. It is the cleverest plan I have ever not made.

complication.logline: The hero attempts a dignified farewell kiss from the top of the stairs and does not stop at the bottom.

lines.text: I shall say farewell with a kiss, from the top of the stairs. Dignified. Heroic. Brief.
That is the banister, {lead}. You are kissing the banister.
It is an excellent banister. It has been waiting its whole life for this.
You are now at the bottom of the stairs. The banister is still at the top. You were not formally introduced.

reversal.logline: It turns out the Wrong Man was the groom all along, which is more than anyone mentioned.

lines.text: Someone must be the groom. The bride has been waiting in the next room since breakfast, with the register.
Me? I only came about the gas meter.
Look at the register! The groom's name is {fool}! Right house, right man, wrong everything else.
I am delighted. And a little frightened. May I sit down on the bed?

reversal.logline: Three people hide in the wardrobe from a fourth person, who is also in the wardrobe.

lines.text: Quick, in the wardrobe! Nobody will look in the wardrobe!
{lead}, I am already in the wardrobe. I got here first. Please remove your elbow from my ear.
I too am in the wardrobe. I came for a coat. I stayed out of loyalty.
Then who is knocking from the back of the wardrobe?

reversal.logline: The hero discovers a handsome but shifty intruder in the bedroom mirror and demands an explanation.

lines.text: There is a stranger in the room! They are wearing my coat! They copy everything I do!
That is a mirror, {lead}.
That is what they want us to think. Look, they are pointing at me. Stop pointing at me!
Please don't shout at the mirror. It is very sensitive. I have been speaking kindly to it all week.

reversal.logline: Great-Uncle Percival has died in the bed, and the wedding must not find out.

lines.text: Great-Uncle Percival has died, quietly, in the bed. If the vicar finds out, the wedding is off.
Then Percival will attend the wedding. As a guest. A very still, very supportive guest.
I have dressed him. He looks marvellous. He has agreed with everything I have said.
Percival was always an excellent listener.

reversal.logline: The hero serenades the bedroom window and, in the dark, the wrong wall.

lines.text: Come to the window, my dearest dove, and hear the song of my undying love... whichever one you are!
That is my bedroom wall. You are serenading plaster.
It is rather a good wall. It has not left yet.
Then I shall continue. It is the most attentive audience I have had all week.

twist.logline: The trunk everyone has been guarding contains the body, which turns out to be potatoes in a good suit.

lines.text: Open the {object}. Slowly. Brace yourselves for the body.
It is not a body. It is potatoes. Very well-dressed potatoes, in Percival's good suit.
Then what have I been burying in the garden all morning?
Probably more potatoes. It is that sort of week.

twist.logline: The deed to the house is found in the cellar, around the neck of a goose.

lines.text: I have found the owner of the house. It is down here. It is wearing the deed around its neck.
That is a goose. A goose cannot own a house. There are laws.
There are no laws on the subject, {villain}. I asked the solicitor to check. Twice.
It has allowed us to stay. It would only like the bread to be better.

twist.logline: The family puts the Wrong Man on trial in the cellar before a jury of twelve unimpressed barrels.

lines.text: Members of the jury: the accused is charged with arriving at the wrong house. How do you plead?
Innocent, by reason of directions. They said 'second left'. This was a second left.
The defence rests, my lord. The jury is twelve barrels, and I believe they were moved.
They have not moved an inch. Guilty, then, of everything.

twist.logline: Music is coming from under the floor. The cellar, it turns out, has a very busy social calendar.

lines.text: Music? Under the floor? Who is dancing in the {place}?
The neighbours, and most of {town}. Every night since the wedding was announced. It is a secret society. They dance.
I am in it. I am the treasurer. Dues are two buttons and a good attitude.
I have always wanted to join a secret society. Is there a casserole rota?

twist.logline: The brother-in-law's great scheme turns out to be a surprise party, which is worse.

lines.text: Why is the cellar full of bunting and a very large cake with my name on it?
It was meant to be a surprise. I have been lying to you for three weeks. It was exhausting.
I was not invited. I came in through the coal chute. May I stay? I brought nothing, but I am very surprised.
You scheming, thoughtful soul. I shall never forgive you. Is it lemon?

finale.logline: Eleven people use seven doors simultaneously, and somehow end up where they started.

lines.text: Everyone out through the doors, calmly, in an orderly fashion, one door each!
There are eleven of us and seven doors. I will take two. I have earned two.
I went out of the front door and in through the window, and now I am the person in the middle.
We are all back in the {place}, from different directions, at once. It is the neatest thing we have ever done.

finale.logline: The wedding goes ahead with the right hat and, by a clerical oversight, the wrong couple.

lines.text: Do you, {lead}, take {fool} to be your lawfully wedded... oh. This is the wrong couple. The list was eaten.
I will if you will, {fool}. I do not know why, but it feels right. It feels damp.
I do. I came to read the gas meter, and I have stayed for the cake.
By the power vested in me by a borrowed hat, I pronounce you both... something. You may kiss, ideally each other.

finale.logline: Lunch is finally served, and the soufflé rises, and rises, and does not stop.

lines.text: Ladies, gentlemen and one goose: lunch is served. Sit where you can. Sit on whom you must.
The soufflé has risen! After eleven attempts, it has risen!
It is still rising, {lead}. It has reached the ceiling.
It has left through the roof. It wishes us all well. It wants to see the world.

finale.logline: Everyone confesses everything at once, and the confessions cancel each other out.

lines.text: I confess! I have two fiancées, a borrowed umbrella, and a deep, abiding fear of the cellar!
I confess! I arranged everything: the wedding, the telegram, the soufflé and the goose!
I confess! I am from the gas board! I do not know why I am saying this so loudly!
Wonderful. Now we all know everything, and nobody has to do anything about it.

finale.logline: The chandelier, which has hung over the whole farce with intent, finally comes down.

lines.text: Does anyone else notice that the chandelier is lower than it was? Considerably lower?
It was bolted to the ceiling. I have the bolts here in my pocket. I thought they were buttons.
Everyone stand perfectly still. Do not breathe. Do not, under any circumstances, ring the doorbell.
...I think that was the doorbell.

name: Whodunit
blurb: A dead host, a helpful butler, and a goose who saw everything and will not be drawn.

setup.logline: His lordship raises a glass, announces that he knows what everyone did, and falls into the soup.

lines.text: His lordship raised his glass, said 'I know what every one of you did,' and fell into the soup.
Then nobody leaves this room. Nobody touches the soup. Nobody touches his lordship.
I touched the soup. It is lovely. It is a little murdery, but very well seasoned.
I should mention that I am the butler, that I was nowhere near the soup, and that nobody asked.

setup.logline: The storm has washed out the bridge, and the front door has locked itself in solidarity.

lines.text: I regret to say the bridge to {town} has gone, the telephone has been eaten, and the weather has locked all the doors.
So we are trapped in a country house with a dead host and no way out?
Not at all. There are eleven ways out. All of them lead into the weather.
I saw the storm lock the front door. It used a key shaped like lightning. I can describe the key.

setup.logline: There are exactly two witnesses to the crime, and one of them is a goose.

lines.text: I saw everything. I was in the corner, quiet as a hat. It happened at 9:41, and it was extremely rude.
What happened at 9:41?
Everything. All of it, one thing after another, in the wrong order. Ask the {object}; it saw more than I did.
The witness is unreliable and the {object} is a goose. I would advise the detective to disregard both.

setup.logline: It is a masked ball, which is a lovely idea until somebody has to be identified.

lines.text: A masked ball. Everyone in a face that is not theirs. How am I to find a murderer in all this?
I have taken the liberty of collecting everyone's masks, shoes and, as a courtesy, their opinions.
I took mine off. There was another underneath. I am three masks deep and I have lost track of who I am.
Splendid. Then the first suspect is whoever asked for the masks. {villain}, please do not leave the room.

setup.logline: Every guest received an invitation reading 'I know what you did.' One of them is from an aunt.

lines.text: Each of you received an invitation reading 'I know what you did.' May I see them?
I received one too. I assumed it was about the soup. It is always about the soup.
Mine says 'I know what you did, and I forgive you, and could you bring a cake.' It is from my aunt.
I will set that one aside.

complication.logline: A second body turns up in the library, between 'Poisons' and 'Poisoners: A Beginner's Guide.'

lines.text: I have found a second body, in the {place}, between 'Poisons' and 'Poisoners: A Beginner's Guide.'
It is Mrs. Grimble, the cook. She knew the recipe for the soup, the wine and, I regret to say, me.
What exactly did she know about you?
Only that I am extremely helpful. I shall fetch some tea and be somewhere else.

complication.logline: The detective leans on a book, the bookcase revolves, and the investigation takes a brief and unplanned turn.

lines.text: This book is conspicuously out of place. It is called 'Do Not Pull This Book.'
Do not pull it. It says so on the spine.
Too late! The bookcase is turning! I am being taken somewhere, in the line of duty, and I shall report back!
I shall note that the detective has gone into the wall. I will fetch the sherry; it is that sort of evening.

complication.logline: The detective interrogates the suspects and obtains two alibis for the same spoon.

lines.text: Where were you at 9:41, {villain}?
In the pantry, polishing a spoon. The spoon will confirm it.
I was also in the pantry. We were not together. We were politely adjacent.
So the spoon was polished twice, by two people who were not together. That spoon has seen more than anyone in this house.

complication.logline: Every clue the detective finds points firmly at the detective.

lines.text: A footprint, size seven. A button from a green coat. A monocle engraved with my initials. How curious.
Look in the mirror, detective. Green coat. Size seven shoes. One monocle. Quite a convincing murderer.
The detective is the culprit. I am shocked. I am also, privately, impressed by the efficiency.
Nonsense. I have been framed. Quite possibly by myself, but still.

complication.logline: A poem is found under the blotter, and it is somehow worse than the murder.

lines.text: His lordship's last word was 'marmalade.' His last poem was worse. 'Roses are red, the soup has gone sour...'
'...I shall be dead within the hour.' It scans! Whoever did it, his lordship died a poet.
Evidence in verse. I have never been so insulted on behalf of the law.
It is signed 'Yours, in agony and iambs.' I believe we are looking for an English teacher.

reversal.logline: The body is the gardener in his lordship's dinner jacket, which raises further questions about the jacket.

lines.text: I looked closely at the body. It is wearing his lordship's dinner jacket. It has the gardener's hands.
So the dead man is not the host.
Then where is the host? And why does the gardener own such a very nice jacket?
Two excellent questions. I shall write them on my cuff and refer to them later.

reversal.logline: The butler's unbreakable alibi turns out to rest on a garden clock that has been wrong since 1923.

lines.text: I can prove I was nowhere near the library at 9:41. The garden clock confirms it.
The garden clock says 9:41. It also says it is Thursday. It has said so since 1923.
I have always liked that clock. It never lies. It simply refuses to move.
I stand by the clock. A clock that does not move is a clock that cannot move against you.

reversal.logline: The motive flips: his lordship was penniless, and the family fortune is a very large stuffed pike.

lines.text: I have found the family fortune. It is in the greenhouse. It is a stuffed pike. The pike is wearing a monocle.
That is the fortune? I thought his lordship was rich!
He was rich in spirit, and in pikes. Mostly in pikes.
Then someone killed him for a pike. I have never been so concerned for a fish.

reversal.logline: The detective and the prime suspect waltz in the greenhouse, strictly in the interests of the investigation.

lines.text: May I have this dance, detective? Purely to establish where everyone was standing at 9:41.
Purely investigatory. One has to be thorough. Mind the geraniums.
I am witnessing this. I do not know what I am witnessing. It is mostly elbows.
I find myself, {villain}, entirely unable to suspect you. This is a serious professional problem.

reversal.logline: The soup is cleared of all charges. The biscuit, however, has a great deal to answer for.

lines.text: The laboratory report is in. The soup was perfectly wholesome. Slightly dull, but wholesome.
I knew it. I said it was only a little murdery. I now apologise to the soup.
Then what was it, detective? A tragic accident? A biscuit?
Oh. Oh no. Why would you say 'a biscuit'? {villain}, why are you holding the biscuit tin?

twist.logline: The Helpful Butler confesses to the murder but insists, in mitigation, that the victim asked.

lines.text: I did it, detective. But I wish it recorded that his lordship asked me to, in writing, with a lovely signature.
He asked to be murdered?
He said it would raise the tone of the weekend. He wanted it done before the bread course.
He did say he wanted to go out with a bang. I thought he meant fireworks.

twist.logline: The goose finally testifies. It honks once, with enormous confidence, in the direction of the biscuit tin.

lines.text: Order! The court calls its only reliable witness. {fool}, please translate.
The goose says: 'HONK.' In my professional opinion, this means 'it was the one with the biscuit tin.'
That is slander. From a goose. In a cellar. At an inconvenient time.
It is the first testimony all night that was not a lie or a poem. Hand over the biscuit tin, {villain}.

twist.logline: The butler removes the whiskers, and it is his lordship, who has been serving the soup for six years.

lines.text: If you take off the whiskers... {villain} is his lordship. Lord Pembry-Wattle has been the butler all along.
I wished to hear what people said when they thought I was not listening. It was a mistake. They said nothing.
Then who is the man in the soup?
A cousin. I am so sorry. I was behind the tureen for most of it and I missed the details.

twist.logline: His lordship's ghost appears in the cellar and points at the culprit, and at everyone else, in turn.

lines.text: Detective, behind you. A ghost, in a dinner jacket, pointing.
Lord Pembry-Wattle! Who did this to you? Point at the culprit!
He is pointing at me. Now at you. Now at {villain}. Now at the wine. Now at {town}, which is eleven miles away.
He is also saying 'marmalade' again. He does that. I believe it is a clue, or a preference.

twist.logline: Behind the wine rack lies the real motive: a crown, a duchy, and a pond.

lines.text: The motive, at last: behind the wine rack, the Crown of Little Mumbling. A duchy of six houses and a pond.
A duchy! Whoever wore that crown would be a duke. Of the pond.
I would murder for a pond. I am not saying I did. I am saying I understand.
The most pathetic motive I have ever heard, and the most believable.

twist.logline: The Helpful Butler produces a sword from the umbrella stand and politely threatens everyone with it.

lines.text: I regret that I must now be unhelpful. Nobody move. This sword has been in the umbrella stand since Easter.
Put it down, {villain}! You are a butler! Butlers do not have swords!
I do not have a licence for it, certainly. But I have a great deal of sympathy for the sword.
For the record, it took four attempts to draw. The umbrella stand held on very bravely.

finale.logline: The detective gathers the suspects and announces that everyone in this room is a suspect, including the room.

lines.text: I have gathered you all in the {place} because everyone in this room is a suspect. Including the room.
The room has an alibi, detective. It was in the house the whole time.
The killer had access to the soup, knew the library, and is at this moment handing round the biscuits.
...I do so like to be useful.

finale.logline: The guilty party is exposed, and the chandelier, sensing a climax, joins in.

lines.text: The weapon was never the soup. It was the chandelier, which has been loose since Tuesday!
I did say it looked lower. I said it to the goose. The goose said nothing.
I did not touch the chandelier. I merely polished it, thoroughly, with intent.
Everybody stand clear of the... oh. It has fallen. It was the only predictable thing all evening.

finale.logline: The detective proposes tea as a test of guilt, and the teapot proposes a goose.

lines.text: The tea is poured. The killer, I believe, will be the one who does not drink it.
I do not take tea. It is a long-standing and entirely unrelated principle.
Everyone will drink, on my count. One, two... why is there a goose in the teapot?
It saw everything. It is trying to leave.

finale.logline: The guilty party flees, and every door in the house turns out to be a cupboard.

lines.text: I shall be leaving by the front door. Do not follow. I have a head start and an umbrella.
Stop! Every exit is guarded!
Detective, that door is a cupboard. That door is a cupboard. That one is a cupboard that thinks it is a door.
This is the third cupboard. I have never been so thoroughly defeated by joinery.

finale.logline: His lordship wakes up. He was only asleep in the soup, and is mortified about the fuss.

lines.text: His lordship has woken up. He was asleep in the soup. He says he is very sorry about the fuss.
Asleep? For three hours? In the soup?
He is a very sound sleeper. I should have mentioned it. I was busy being suspicious.
Then I have solved nothing. I shall bill for the weekend regardless.

name: Gothic Romance
blurb: Moors, candles and a ghost who is mostly disappointed. Everyone is brooding; some of them on time.

roles.villain: The Brooding Master of the House

setup.logline: The new governess crosses the moor in a storm, clutching a letter of reference that has not survived the rain.

lines.text: The directions said 'just past the second gorse bush.' I have passed eleven. They were all rather sinister.
It is the house with the light on. Do not go in. I would say that more ominously if I had the energy.
You are late. The last governess was late too. She is in the walls now, I think. She sends her regards.
I carry a letter of reference from the Bishop of Mumbling. It has, regrettably, become a puddle.

setup.logline: A figure on the hill broods at the horizon, in the rain, without an umbrella.

lines.text: There is a figure on the hill, gazing at the horizon as though it owed them money.
That is {villain}, who has been brooding since Tuesday. It is a thorough job.
I am contemplating a loss I cannot name.
Is it the umbrella? You seem to have lost the umbrella.

setup.logline: The front door opens by itself, which is a ghost's way of saying 'I suppose you had better come in.'

lines.text: Oooooh. Welcome. I am the ghost. I was going to rattle some chains, but they are in the wash.
A ghost! How marvellous. Are you going to haunt me?
I was going to. I have been trying since Tuesday. I am not very good. Nobody has been frightened since the Regency.
Do not encourage the ghost, {lead}. It will want to discuss its feelings.

setup.logline: Someone is singing in the closed west wing, very sincerely and about a quarter-tone flat.

lines.text: I can hear someone singing in the west wing. Very softly. Terribly flat.
There is nobody in the west wing. The door has been locked for years, and also for reasons.
That is me. I am practising. It is 'The Last Rose of Summer', but the rose keeps going off-key.
A ghost, singing flat, in a closed wing, for reasons. I could not be more delighted.

setup.logline: Tea is served on the moor in a gale, because the family believes in the weather.

lines.text: Tea is served on the moor. It has been served on the moor since 1790. The weather is part of the family.
May we take it indoors? My cup is full of sideways rain.
I have attended this tea for two hundred years. The rain has not improved.
Then we shall observe a minute of silence for the scones, which have blown to Norfolk.

complication.logline: The governess descends the grand staircase with dignity and is caught at the bottom by the master of the house.

lines.text: I shall descend the grand staircase with dignity, composure and the {object}...
Mind the third step. It has taken a governess before.
You caught me. You have caught me quite by accident, and with surprisingly gentle hands.
I did not push you. I merely sighed in your direction. It is a very draughty staircase.

complication.logline: The harp plays itself in the empty ballroom, badly, and the master asks the governess to dance.

lines.text: The harp is playing itself again. Badly. It is usually a waltz. Will you... dance?
I do not waltz. I have only ever danced with a coat stand, at school.
I would play the harp, but I have no hands. I shall do it mostly with mood.
Then let us be bad at it together.

complication.logline: A ghost is perched on the great chandelier, sulking in the draught.

lines.text: There is a ghost on the {object}. It appears to be sulking.
I am not sulking. I am perching with disappointment. I have been up here since 1823 and no one has once looked up.
Do not stand beneath it, {lead}. It has fallen on two governesses and a delegation from {town}. We keep a ledger.
Then I shall admire it from the doorway, with great respect and a small umbrella.

complication.logline: The governess finds a letter in which the master of the house requests, from the Bishop, a dog instead of a governess.

lines.text: I found a letter in the hall, addressed to the Bishop. 'Do not send me a governess. Send me a dog. A calm one.'
That was written before I met you. I would like to amend it: send me a dog and a governess.
{villain} has been writing it for years. I proofread. The dog was my suggestion.
I am not offended. I am slightly offended. But mostly I am flattered by the dog.

complication.logline: The great hall's fire will not light, because there is a storm in the chimney and the candle has opinions.

lines.text: The fire will not light. There is a storm in the chimney. It has been there since Tuesday.
I could light it with this candle.
Oooh. The candle went out. That is the tenth time today. It is a very good effect. I am jealous.
It happens whenever anyone says something hopeful in this house.

complication.logline: The ghost tries to pull a chair out from under the governess. The chair, and the ghost, have other plans.

lines.text: I have decided to haunt you properly. I shall move this chair. Watch closely. It is a very frightening chair.
I am watching. Oh, it moves. How unsettling. I shall sit down, to steady myself.
Not there! That is where I... oh. You have sat on the ghost. I am now underneath you.
Do not apologise, {lead}. It is the first time in two hundred years that anything has frightened the ghost.

reversal.logline: The master's diary reveals the house's terrible secret: a goose.

lines.text: I found your diary. 'Today I stared at the moor again. I was not looking at the moor. I was watching for the goose.'
It is a very large goose. It has a look. I have not set foot on the moor in eleven years.
I have met the goose. It is quite nice. It only wants to be loved, and also your hat.
So the dark secret of the house is a goose. I feel strangely relieved, and slightly cheated.

reversal.logline: The portrait of the woman the master lost is revealed to be a portrait of a pony.

lines.text: That portrait is of the woman I lost, {lead}. You are the image of her. Same cheekbones. Same disapproving eyebrow.
That is not a woman. That is Dorothea, the pony. The family is very attached.
She was a good pony. She had a way of looking at one.
Then I am honoured to resemble Dorothea.

reversal.logline: The master of the house tries to declare an affection and can only do it in rhyme.

lines.text: I cannot say it plainly, so I shall say it in rhyme: I find you quite agreeable, most of the time.
That is the most romantic thing anyone has ever said to me, and it scanned.
I have a drawer of poems. Everything rhymes with 'moor'. I have been to the very bottom of 'more'.
I wrote half of them. 'Door' and 'floor' were mine. 'Gore' was entirely {villain}'s.

reversal.logline: The Bishop of Mumbling arrives to examine the governess's credentials, which are a puddle.

lines.text: The Bishop of Mumbling has arrived to examine your credentials, {lead}. He is in the library with a clipboard.
I have excellent credentials. I have a letter. It is a puddle, but it is a very distinguished puddle.
I looked over the Bishop's shoulder. He has written 'Governess: unqualified. Lovely smile.' All on one line.
I have decided to overlook the first part.

reversal.logline: The master unmasks to reveal the terrible scar that has shaped everything, and it is a pencil mark.

lines.text: You wear a mask in the house, {villain}. I think I deserve to know why.
Beneath this mask is a terrible scar. A duel. A storm. A great betrayal.
It is a pencil mark. {villain} sat on a pencil at school, in a hurry.
It was a very sharp pencil, {fool}. Do not mock the pencil.

reversal.logline: The master challenges the ghost to a duel over a review of some poetry. Neither can hit the other.

lines.text: Ghost, you insulted my verse! I shall make your afterlife worse! En garde!
I said it was 'a bold use of the word moor'. That is not an insult. That is a review.
Please, both of you. One of you cannot be hit, and the other cannot hit.
The sword goes straight through you, {fool}. It is the most insulting thing that has ever happened to my sword.

twist.logline: The attic is full of love letters addressed to a governess the master had not yet met.

lines.text: The attic is full of letters. Hundreds of them. All addressed to 'The Governess I Have Not Yet Met.'
I wrote one every night. It is a hobby. I realise it is not a conventional hobby.
There are also forty-one addressed to 'The Dog.' {villain} was very optimistic.
Then I am, apparently, the first reply.

twist.logline: The attic mirror reflects only the governess, which is two reflections fewer than anyone had prepared for.

lines.text: The mirror shows only me. It does not show you, {fool}, which I expected. It does not show you, {villain}, which I did not.
...I had hoped to raise it at a more suitable moment. I am also a ghost. It has been a long time. I did not like to say.
Since 1871. I promised not to tell. I am bad at secrets but excellent at not bothering.
Then the brooding was not a character flaw. It was a lifestyle.

twist.logline: The family silver is found in the attic, and the thief is the household ghost.

lines.text: The attic contains the family silver. Every spoon. Two hundred years' worth.
I can explain. I was lonely. A ghost needs something to hold. Spoons are excellent company.
I thought the burglars were thorough. It was you, {fool}. You have been robbing us from the inside.
From beyond, actually. It is different. There is a lot of paperwork.

twist.logline: The governess confesses to being an acrobat, and the chandelier is mentioned with interest.

lines.text: I must confess something. I am not a qualified governess. I am a trained acrobat. The references were my cousin's.
That explains the window on the first night. And the banister. I thought it was the draught.
I am so sorry. I could teach the children the trapeze, if there are any children.
There are no children. But there is a very sturdy chandelier.

twist.logline: Uncle Ambrose is found in the attic rocking chair, wearing a cardigan and a long silence.

lines.text: In the rocking chair there is a skeleton, wearing a very nice cardigan.
That is Uncle Ambrose. He did not like to be moved. He has been very consistent about it.
I know him! We were at school together. He is the reason I became a ghost. He made it look so easy.
He is very still. He is the best houseguest I have ever had.

finale.logline: The wedding takes place in the graveyard, with a vicar, a ghost and an unconvincing rain machine.

lines.text: I, {villain}, take you, {lead}, to be my governess, my companion and my reason to come in from the rain.
I, {lead}, take you. I should like it noted that I am doing so under a very small umbrella.
I object! No, wait, I do not. I have always wanted to say that. I object to nothing. It is lovely.
Then by the authority of the moor, and a vicar in a hat, I suppose we are married.

finale.logline: At last the master says it aloud, and the sky can think of nothing to add but lightning.

lines.text: I have waited my whole life to say it. I love you, {lead}. There. The sky may now do as it likes.
That is the best lightning I have ever seen, and I was here for the 1790s.
Then kiss me quickly, before the weather gets any better.
Sorry. I am standing on {villain}'s foot. I was trying to be supportive.

finale.logline: The household ghost is finally laid to rest, mildly disappointed that it was not harder.

lines.text: I think it has worked. I am... going. I always thought it would be more dramatic.
You were a wonderful ghost, {fool}. The best I have ever had.
I am the only one you have ever had. But thank you. It is the first review I have ever received.
Let us sing. It is customary. Somebody start the hymn, and start it badly, for {fool}.

finale.logline: The master of the house delivers a long-awaited speech on love and loss. It is short.

lines.text: I have a few words to say about love and loss. They are: love, and loss.
That was beautiful. Is there more?
No. That is the full text. I have been working on it for years.
It is the best speech anyone has given in this graveyard. And I have heard the one about the fox.

finale.logline: The previous governess emerges from the churchyard wall with a clipboard, a grievance and no tea.

lines.text: The previous governess has come out of the churchyard wall. She has a clipboard. She has notes.
Hello. I do hope you were not too uncomfortable in there.
She is very cross. She says the wall is damp, the company poor, and the biscuits a long time ago.
May I offer you tea? I am told the ghost makes a decent one, mostly by sighing at the kettle.

name: Pantomime
blurb: He's behind you! A dame, a cow in two halves, and a great deal of shouting.

setup.logline: The village goose lays a golden egg, and it is in the wrong hands before the applause has finished.

lines.text: Good morning, boys and girls! Look, our little goose has laid an egg! A golden one! Nobody tell the Baron!
Did somebody say Baron? Do not bother to boo, I have had my breakfast. I shall simply take the egg.
Put it down, Baron! It belongs to the village and to the goose's many friends!
The goose says it was a one-off. She is retiring. She wants to go into catering.

setup.logline: The Dame enters in a hat shaped like a cottage loaf and delivers eleven puns, none of them necessary.

lines.text: Hello, boys and girls! I am the Dame! I have just come from the baker's. I was feeling a bit crusty!
Good morning, Dame. That is a very large hat.
It is a loaf, dear. I wore it to sell the bread. I was selling like hot... rolls!
I have been a wicked baron for thirty years, and I have never heard a pun that hurt like that.

setup.logline: The whole village launches into the opening number, and the Baron attends purely to ruin it.

lines.text: Good morning, {town}! It is a lovely day for a song and a dance!
Everybody on the green! Left foot! Right foot! Other left foot! I only have two, but I am trying!
I hate this. The singing. The dancing. The rhyming. I shall ruin it, and I shall do it in time to the music.
Then join us, Baron! The chorus has a part for a villain. It is mostly 'boo'.

setup.logline: Buttercup the cow enters in two halves, who immediately disagree about the direction of the play.

lines.text: Everybody say hello to Buttercup, our cow! Front half, wave. Back half... lift your tail, dear.
She seems to be walking in two directions at once.
That is the back half. It wants the pantry. The front half wants the barn. They are both correct.
It is the first time she has given a straight answer. Well, a straight half-answer.

setup.logline: The King decrees that whoever finds the golden egg may marry the Principal Boy. Nobody tells the Principal Boy.

lines.text: Oyez, oyez, boys and girls! By order of the King: whoever finds the golden egg may marry the Principal Boy!
Has anyone asked the Principal Boy?
Nobody asks the Principal Boy. It is tradition. Nobody asks the egg either.
I did ask the egg. It seemed keen. It also seemed like an egg.

complication.logline: The Baron creeps up behind the Principal Boy, and the audience has several suggestions.

lines.text: Is somebody behind me, boys and girls? Because I have a funny feeling about the back of my head.
He is behind you! Behind you! No, the other behind!
I am merely standing here. I am doing nothing. If the Principal Boy turns around, I shall have to turn around too.
I am turning! He is turning! We are all turning! This is the longest circle I have ever made.

complication.logline: The Baron's banquet is musical chairs with one chair, twelve guests and no clear exit strategy.

lines.text: Welcome to my banquet. Please take a seat. There are twelve guests and one chair. It is a game. I call it 'Dinner'.
It is musical chairs! Boys and girls, start the music! When it stops, sit on the nearest Baron!
Dum de dum dum... somebody stop the music!
Get off me, {fool}. I am a villain with a bad back. We are the most dangerous kind.

complication.logline: The Baron consults the magic mirror and receives, for the first time, a complaint.

lines.text: Magic mirror, tell me true: who is the loveliest in the land?
It says... hang on... 'Please can you stop leaning on the glass.'
That is not a mirror! That is the back half of Buttercup in a picture frame!
It is a very good frame. It is the only part of this castle I paid for.

complication.logline: A sword fight is conducted entirely in rhyming couplets, and the Baron runs out of rhymes before the sword.

lines.text: En garde, you wretched Principal Boy! I will make you sorry! I will make you cry! I will run you over with a... lorry?
That is a modern vehicle, Baron. We are in the Middle Ages.
It is the rhyme's fault, dear! {villain} is under pressure! Everybody help! What rhymes with 'sorry'?
Do not ask them. They will say 'lorry'.

complication.logline: The Baron disguises as the Good Fairy, wearing wings made from a dustpan.

lines.text: Greetings, children! I am the Good Fairy! I am not the Baron. I am a perfectly different shape.
Good Fairy, you are wearing a wicked cloak and three days of beard.
Fairies are naturally scruffy. It is the wings. They take it out of one.
Boys and girls, is that the Good Fairy? I can't hear you! IS THAT THE GOOD FAIRY?

reversal.logline: At the ball the Baron asks the Dame to dance, and everyone agrees to pretend this is normal.

lines.text: Dame, may I have the honour? I have been a villain for forty years, and I should like to be a nuisance in a different way.
Oh, Baron! I have not danced since the Great Pudding Fire!
Boys and girls, the Baron is in love with the Dame! This is either a triumph or a very large mistake!
Do not mock this, Principal Boy. The Dame has beautiful hands, and I intend to kiss both of them.

reversal.logline: At the masked ball everyone is unmasked on the count of three, to a disappointing silence.

lines.text: Everyone take off your masks on the count of three! One, two, three!
My mask is off! Oh. It is still me. It is me underneath. I was hoping for somebody more glamorous.
Mine is off too. Underneath is a smaller, sadder Baron. Please do not look.
And mine... oh. It is all of us. Nobody is anyone else. This is the dullest unmasking in the history of balls.

reversal.logline: The Principal Boy swings out on the ballroom chandelier, which turns out to have been sold.

lines.text: Stand back! I shall swing across the ballroom on the chandelier and rescue the Dame!
Be careful, dear, it is an antique! It is from the age before swinging!
It is no longer attached to anything. I sold it on Tuesday. The buyer collects at eight.
That would explain why I am taking the ceiling with me.

reversal.logline: The Baron tries a clog on every foot in the kingdom, and it fits the back half of a cow.

lines.text: Whoever fits this clog is the rightful heir! Everyone form a queue on the stairs! One foot at a time!
It fits Buttercup's back left! Oh, what a terrible thing to happen to a cow!
The heir to the throne is a cow!
The back half of a cow. I demand a recount.

reversal.logline: The sing-along begins, and the Baron joins in for a boiled sweet, to everyone's surprise, especially the Baron's.

lines.text: Boys and girls, it is time for the sing-along! The words are on the banner! Left side, you are the Baron's team!
I refuse to sing. I am wicked. I have standards. ...Oh, there is a prize? What kind of prize?
A boiled sweet! Whoever sings loudest wins a boiled sweet!
Then I shall sing. Tell the boys and girls to stop making that noise. ...Oh. That is me making that noise.

reversal.logline: The Baron dies, spectacularly and repeatedly, and keeps opening one eye to check the reviews.

lines.text: Aargh! I am slain! I am dead! I have never been so dead in all my life!
Boys and girls, is the Baron dead? Oh no he isn't! Oh yes he is! Oh no he isn't! I can't keep up!
The Baron has been dead for three minutes, and has opened one eye to check whether we are watching.
I am still dead. I am only resting my eyes. I shall be dead again in the finale.

twist.logline: A ghost drifts through the cellar, and the Dame is the only one who cannot see it.

lines.text: Oooh, it is spooky down here! Boys and girls, is there a ghost? I don't see a ghost!
There is a ghost behind you, Dame!
Where? Oh no there isn't! Oh, there is! It has gone through the door, and me, and the Baron!
I felt that. It was clammy. I request that the ghost apologise.

twist.logline: It is discovered that the goose has been the Good Fairy all along, and the Baron has been tying her to a fence.

lines.text: I have just had a thought, boys and girls. Has anybody ever seen the goose and the Good Fairy in the same room?
Never! Do you mean the goose...
...is the Good Fairy? I have been tying a fairy to a fence post for three years.
She is very forgiving. She would like to be untied now, please, and also a sandwich.

twist.logline: The Baron's deadly potion turns out to be lemonade, and the lemonade turns out to be the plot.

lines.text: Behold! The {object}! One sip and you shall be turned into... into... something worse.
Is it a toad, Baron? A newt? A very small bishop?
It is lemonade. I mixed up the labels. Give it back; that was to be my elevenses.
So the poison is lemonade, and the lemonade is poison. Boys and girls, that is what we call a sour twist.

twist.logline: The Dame is revealed as the Baron's double agent, to the surprise of everyone except the audience.

lines.text: Dame! You have been helping the Baron all this time?
Oh, I can explain, dear. The pay is terrible, but the hat budget is marvellous.
The Dame has been my double agent for eleven years. Paid in buns.
Boys and girls, did you know about this? You did? Then why didn't you shout?

twist.logline: A dragon named Gerald guards the cellar. It has a cough, and every cough costs somebody a wig.

lines.text: The cellar is guarded by a fire-breathing dragon. It is called Gerald.
Gerald is lovely! He has a bad cough, though. Every time he coughs, somebody's wig goes up.
Everyone back! I can feel the heat! I am only a Principal Boy and I am not insured!
It has my wig. It has my good wig. Somebody fetch the second-best wig.

finale.logline: The Baron is beaten, the goose is free, and the whole cast gets married at once, mostly to each other.

lines.text: Boys and girls, the Baron is beaten, the goose is free, and we are going to have a wedding!
Who is marrying whom? Nobody has told me! I was only told to wear this!
I am to marry the Dame, which is the best-run plot twist of the evening, and I stand by it.
Then let us sing the wedding song! Everybody! Left side, right side, and the people in the middle who always forget!

finale.logline: The traditional slosh scene begins with forty custard pies and ends with everyone the same colour.

lines.text: And now the traditional slosh scene! I have prepared forty custard pies and one very polite bucket!
I refuse to be hit by a pie. I have dignity. I have a reputation. I have... oh. Oh, I have a pie.
Boys and girls, shall we? Three, two, one! Aim for the Baron, but be kind to the bucket!
Everybody is covered! Even the bucket is covered! We are all the same colour! It is beautiful!

finale.logline: The King abdicates in favour of the goose, which accepts with the dignity of a creature that expected nothing less.

lines.text: People of {town}: the King has been found, and he has abdicated in favour of the goose.
The goose is wearing the crown! It looks wonderful! It looks like it has been waiting all its life!
A goose queen. I am too tired to object. I shall be a loyal subject, as soon as somebody finds me a chair.
Long live the goose! Boys and girls, you know the next bit! Long live the...

finale.logline: The Dame delivers the traditional closing couplet in place of the Good Fairy, who is off sick.

lines.text: The Good Fairy is off sick, so: the play is done, the day is won, the Baron's gone, and we've had fun!
It lacks a moral.
Then here is one: never tie a fairy to a fence.
That does not rhyme, but it is true, which is better.

finale.logline: Buttercup the cow finally agrees on a direction, which is two directions, and goes.

lines.text: And finally, boys and girls, Buttercup the cow has decided where she is going!
Which way, Buttercup?
Front half, left. Back half, the pub. They have parted. It is the happiest break-up I have ever seen.
She will be fine! She is two cows now! Wave goodbye to the front half! And to the back half, who does not care!
